rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the fact block and gives four genuinely different reporter jobs: founder return, public-company metric, product-principle conflict, and hands-on test. Its headline "Bumble says women still message first. Now the AI can write the message." is the cleanest angle here because the tension is sitting in Bumble's own announcement. B has useful bones, but "Dating apps add AI to write your opening line — and some users hate it" turns one company into a category trend, and "the Dorsey/Schultz/Kalanick-adjacent storyline" drags in borrowed drama the update did not earn.
gaps_in_A: "it is the first product the returned founder has put their name on since coming back this year" goes a half-step past the facts; the update says the relaunch is under the returned founder-CEO, not that it is her first product.
"one concrete decision the founder made in the relaunch that the previous leadership would not have made" is sharp, but it asks for a counterfactual that may be impossible to prove cleanly.
"customer-story" is mislabeled for "What happens when Bumble's AI writes your opening line"; this is a hands-on product test unless you have a real user with permission to tell the story.
gaps_in_B: "Dating apps add AI to write your opening line" pluralizes a single Bumble relaunch into an industry trend. B cautions against that later, but the headline already overclaims.
"the Dorsey/Schultz/Kalanick-adjacent storyline" is lazy comparison scaffolding, not evidence. Also, Kalanick is a messy analogue for a founder-return frame.
"she" and "the company she built" rely on outside knowledge not supplied in the update; in a blind grounding test, that is leakage.
"some users hate it" inflates "some users have criticized AI in dating as inauthentic" into a stronger emotional claim than the facts support.
